faqs.q: What should I include on a tile job estimate?
faqs.a: At minimum: your business name and license number, the client and job-site address, a dated line-item list (installation per sq ft, labor, grouting, demo, waterproofing, materials), a validity date, deposit terms, and exclusions. Note that the estimate is not a final invoice — final charges may vary with substrate condition and layout complexity.

faqs.q: How do I estimate a tile job?
faqs.a: Measure the square footage of each surface to be tiled (length × height for walls, length × width for floors). Multiply by your per-sq-ft installation rate, then add labor hours, grouting, demo, waterproofing, and materials. Add 10–15% waste allowance for cuts and breakage. Put each on its own line so the customer can see the breakdown.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate the deposit automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantities and rates, and the subtotal, 25% deposit and balance due update automatically.

faqs.q: Is this legal or tax advice?
faqs.a: No. Templates are for informational purposes only. Requirements vary by state — verify with your contractor board and a CPA or attorney before use.

faqs.q: How do you calculate how much tile to order?
faqs.a: Measure the area, add the waste factor for the layout, then round up to full boxes. Straight lay in a rectangular room needs 10 percent; diagonal needs 15 percent; herringbone and chevron need 20 to 25. Large-format tile and multiple dye lots each add a further 5 percent. Order all tile for one room from a single dye lot — a box from a different lot will not match, and no waste factor protects you from that.

faqs.q: What does a tile setter charge per square foot?
faqs.a: Installation labour typically runs $4 to $12 per square foot for floor tile and $7 to $20 for wall tile, with the range driven by tile size, layout complexity, substrate condition and whether waterproofing is required. Mosaic and large-format tile sit at the top of the range because they are slow. Heated floors, niche framing and curbless shower conversions are usually priced as separate line items rather than folded into the square-foot rate.

faqs.q: Should waterproofing be a separate line on the estimate?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the line customers most often ask about, because until a shower leaks they do not see the value. Show the membrane, the coverage area, and whether the substrate was prepared first. On a curbless or steam shower, waterproofing and slope work can exceed the cost of the tile itself. Bundling it into a generic install rate hides the work and invites a request to remove it.

faqs.q: How do I price demolition of existing tile?
faqs.a: Per square foot, separately from installation, because it is unpredictable. $2 to $5 per square foot is typical for floor tile over a sound substrate; considerably more when the tile is set in a thick mortar bed, bonded to a slab, or when the substrate will not survive removal. Always state on the estimate that the price assumes the substrate is reusable, and that replacement is billed as a change order.

faqs.q: What payment schedule is normal for a tiling job?
faqs.a: Deposit on acceptance covering material, progress payment when tiling is complete but before grout, balance on final clean and walkthrough. On a bathroom remodel the deposit typically covers tile and membrane, which is the majority of the material cost. Tying each payment to a milestone the customer can see — membrane installed, tile set, grouted and cleaned — makes the schedule easy to accept.

faqs.q: How do I handle a customer-supplied tile job?
faqs.a: Quote labour only, and state two things on the estimate: that you are not responsible for the quantity supplied, and that tile breakage, shading variation and dye-lot mismatch are the customer's risk. Also set a rate for time lost to insufficient quantity, because the second trip to collect more tile after the customer under-ordered is common and unpaid unless it was priced in advance.

deepDive.heading: Tiling estimates that survive the layout argument: waste, substrate and setting materials
deepDive.sub: Tile is the one trade where the customer can count the boxes on the invoice and compare them to the floor. These are the numbers that make a tile estimate defensible — and the ones contractors forget to charge for.

blocks.h3: Waste factor is not optional: 10% straight lay, 15% diagonal, 20%+ for patterns
paras: Every tiling estimate starts with net square footage and then applies a waste factor, because tile is cut at the perimeter, at doorways, around fixtures and on any run that has to be laid out symmetrically. Straight lay in a rectangular room loses about 10%. Diagonal or 45-degree lay loses 15%. Herringbone, chevron and any pattern that repeats on a fixed module loses 20% or more, because you cannot use offcuts from one repeat in another.

Show the waste on the estimate as a separate line: "tile — 180 sq ft installed, 198 sq ft supplied (10% waste)". When the customer later asks why they paid for 20 extra square feet, the answer is already on the page. Contractors who bury waste in the rate field the same question with no answer.

rows: Cuts at every wall become triangles
Multiple rooms with separate dye lots
One box per lot for future repair

blocks.h3: Substrate and preparation are frequently larger than the tile labour
paras: Tile does not go onto a subfloor or wall as found. A wood subfloor needs deflection checked against the tile's L-rating, then a cement backer board or an uncoupling membrane. A slab needs flatness checked to 1/8 inch in 10 feet; anything worse needs self-levelling compound before a single tile goes down. A shower needs a waterproofing membrane and a sloped pan, and that waterproofing is a separate trade skill that many tile setters subcontract.

Estimate preparation as its own block of hours, not as a line item called "prep". Demo of existing tile, backer board installation, levelling, waterproofing and drain work each take measurable time, and a customer who sees them itemized understands why their bathroom estimate is not just square footage times a rate.
list: Demo and haul-away of existing tile: billed per square foot, plus disposal
Cement board or uncoupling membrane: material plus install time
Self-levelling compound: priced per bag plus labour, only when flatness fails
Waterproofing in wet areas: membrane, banding, corners, drain collar
Deflection check on wood subframes — if it fails, the tile job cannot proceed

blocks.h3: Setting materials are a real cost line, and the customer's tile choice changes it
paras: Thinset is not one product. A modified thinset for porcelain over cement board, an unmodified for a membrane that requires it, an epoxy or urethane grout for a commercial kitchen, a large-format-specific mortar for a 24x48 tile — each costs materially more than the bag at the bottom of the price list. Grout and sealant are separate again, and epoxy grout can cost five times a cement grout.

Bill materials as a line, not folded into a per-square-foot labour rate, and note the specification: "modified thinset, 1/2 in notch, epoxy grout per owner request". When the customer supplies their own tile, say so explicitly and state that setting materials and labour are still yours — that keeps a supplied-tile job from looking like an error when the total is only slightly lower than the full quote.
list: Thinset type tied to tile and substrate: modified, unmodified, large-format, rapid-set
Grout: cement vs epoxy vs urethane — epoxy can be 3-5x the material cost
Sealant at changes of plane instead of grout: it is what stops the crack
Trim, Schluter profiles and thresholds: small items, real money across a whole house

blocks.h3: Layout, niches and the details customers remember
paras: Layout time is where a tiling job is won or lost. Centring a pattern, aligning joints across a doorway, matching a niche to the surrounding grid, wrapping a corner so the pattern continues — each is planning work done before the first tile is set, and none of it is square footage.

Price niches, benches, curbs and shelves as each-items rather than including them in the wall rate. A shower niche takes an hour and a half of careful cutting and waterproofing; a bench is framing, board, membrane and tile. Customers add these mid-job, and a contractor who priced them at zero has donated the time.
list: Layout and dry-lay: 1-2 hours on a typical bathroom, more on a patterned floor
Niche: priced each, including waterproofing and trim
Bench, curb, half wall: framing plus board plus membrane plus tile
Grout lines: state the joint width and whether they are sanded or unsanded

blocks.h3: Payment structure and the punch list
paras: Tile work is material-heavy at the start and detail-heavy at the end, which makes the payment schedule matter. A typical split is a deposit to order tile and materials, a progress payment when the floor or walls are set, and a final payment after grouting and cleanup. Holding the last 10 percent until the customer signs off the punch list protects both sides — it gives them a reason to inspect promptly and gives you a reason to finish the details.

Put the punch list on the final invoice as items with dates, and photograph the finished work before you leave. Tile disputes are almost always about a lippage issue, a hollow-sounding tile or a grout line that does not align — and a photograph taken at handover with the customer present ends most of them before they start.
list: Deposit on material order, progress payment at set, final after grout and clean
Photograph finished tile, especially wet areas, before leaving
State the cure time before sealing or heavy use — grout and sealant both have one
